Regulating the Wood Trade and Forestry: Timber Tariffs in Imperial Germany (1870s–1910s)
abstract: In the mid-nineteenth century, when Germany turned into the second-largest wood-importing nation in Europe, political and social tensions arose over the wood trade. In 1879, along with iron and grain, timber became one of the main commodities on which the protectionist compromise between landowners and heavy industry was based. Subsequently, Germany reformed timber tariffs several times – including railway tariffs and criteria for classifying wood types – thereby sparking heated controversies in domestic politics, academic debates among forest scientists and changes in international relations …

title: Exploring Biting as a Form of Relational Response – An Ethnography With Mirā the Horse
abstract: Abstract Influenced by Natural Horsemanship ( NH ), the Japan Racing Association frames biting as a behavioral issue rooted in instinct, correctable through training. This paper draws on a four-month ethnographic encounter with a retired racehorse labeled a “biter” to challenge such framing. Using Itō Asa’s concepts of dentatsu (conveying) and seisei (generative) communication, it argues that defining biting as instinct triggers a closed loop of understanding that reduces horses to behavioral types. In contrast, approaching biting as a relational, context-dependent act enables a seisei mode …

title: Artillo Freeman’s Uniform
abstract: It is the summer of 1820 in New York City. We are in the home—perhaps just a single room—of a ninety-nine-year-old man named Artillo Freeman. He lives with his eighty-eight-year-old wife and disabled thirty-year-old daughter Hester. Freeman has, in the words of the pension application he is preparing, “no Trade, but Picks Oakum for a living when able to Work.” This small task, prizing apart old rope into a fuzzy substance used for caulking (filling) the seams between wooden ship components and for other purposes, is all he is capable of these days. Freeman “is commonly called a black man.” …

title: West of Eden: Race and the Ottoman Armenian roots of California agriculture
abstract: Abstract This article links the transnational environmental history of agriculture with the history of racial formation and immigration in the United States. Focusing on the San Joaquin Valley of California and its global connections, the account explains how the region’s nascent late-nineteenth-century bounty derived in part from both crops and people with origins in the Ottoman empire. Seeds for figs, grapes, and melons all made their way from the Ottoman empire to the United States, and so, too, did Armenians. title: “THE NORMAL EXCEPTION”: EDOARDO GRENDI, MICROANALYSIS, AND GENERALIZATIONS*
abstract: ABSTRACT “The normal exception” has long been a slogan of microhistory. This oxymoronic phrase is the iconic rendering of an incidental sentence that appeared in a 1977 article by Edoardo Grendi. His article, titled “Micro‐analisi e storia sociale” (Microanalysis and Social History), is cited more often than it is read. In this issue of History and Theory , Grendi's seminal article appears in English for the first time. abstract: This article examines the diaries and memoir written by an Australian soldier who fought in the Second World War (1939-1945) and who served in the British Commonwealth Occupation Force (BCOF) in the Occupation of Japan. abstract: Abstract This article brings together two stories of 1970s Mexico that are often narrated separately: the story of the PRI’s attempts to reform itself, specifically through the right to know, and the story of activists’ mobilizations against disappearances. title: Tools and regalia: a short survey of the presence of firearms in Edo Japan
abstract: Abstract Between the arrival of firearms in Japan in 1543 and the crushing of the Shimabara rebellion in 1638, Japan transformed from a fractured country in a permanent state of war into a centralized, peaceful era. However, this was only possible thanks to several transformations made by the Tokugawa regime, not least the firearm itself. The copious amounts of firearms existing in Japan became a domesticated and common element of the Edo period and were prevalent in the country’s transformation. abstract: Abstract There has been extensive research on the phenomenon of code switching, meaning the use of two or more languages or language varieties, within texts. abstract: This study qualitatively analyses the reception of Japanese anime ‘Yuri!!! on ICE’ (YOI) within Japanese fandom using in-depth interviews, content analysis, and participant observation. abstract: This article explores hunting in interwar Greece as a window into the technocratic management of wild fauna and the rise of game as a form of economic capital. abstract: 従来の日タイ関係史研究において、タイに所蔵される日本関連の写真史料は、文書史料を視覚的に補完する「挿絵」的位置づけにとどまり、一次史料として十分に活用されてこなかった。しかし写真史料は、衣装や空間配置、身体表現など、文書では詳述されない視覚的要素を提供する貴重な資料である。 そこで本研究ノートは、タイ国立公文書館「ワチラヤーン図書館と個人コレクション」棚に所蔵されるラーマ五世王・六世王期（1868～1925年）の日本関連写真に焦点をあてた。特に引出し番号18「個人（外国人）」と19「写真家」の目録カードを整理し、日本関連写真の全体像を明らかにした。 分析の結果、「個人（外国人）」には95名の外国人に関する写真情報があり、そのうち日本人は政尾藤吉、稲垣満次郎、細谷善助の3名のみであった。また「写真家」にはラーマ五世・六世王期の写真が105枚あり、そのうち細谷善助アルバム内の写真が96枚と約9割を占めていた。 …

title: ある日本人ジャーナリストの眼に映った近代中国 : 一九一〇～一九三〇年代の神田正雄を中心に
abstract: 本論文はかつて朝日新聞社に所属した中国専門の記者であった神田正雄を取り上げ、1910～1930年代におけるその活動と対中認識を論ずるものである。神田は記事、評論及び著書を通して、近代の日中関係に深く関わったほか、嶺南区域に特別な関心を持ち、世論に大きな影響を与えた人物の一人であった。 本論文では、主に四つの部分に分けて論じる。まずは、拠り所となる基本資料を紹介しながら、近代中国における神田を代表とする日本人ジャーナリストの活動状況を考察した。次に、早稲田大学在学中の中国人留学生との関わりを探り、神田の中国への関与の端緒を解明する。特に、日本人教育顧問兼教習として赴任した、四川省重慶府永川の達用学堂での活躍は高く評価されている。その上で、朝日新聞の北京特派員として対華二十一か条要求をスクープしたことに焦点を当て、1910年代における日中外交の折衝過程を描きながら、「国策」と「民意」とのはざまに置かれた神田の「真意」を探るべく考察した。最後に、視線を嶺南区域に移し、民国時期「西南派」の本拠地に注目して、神田のこの区域に対する関心の高さの理由を解明しつつ、その時の中央政府と地方勢力間の軋轢を日本に有利に動くように工夫する姿勢を検証する。かつて中国の独立や発展を真剣に考えていたであろう神田も時代とともに考えも変化し、戦時のナショナリズムの波から逃れることはできなかった。

abstract: 本稿では、まず村田孜郎の回想文「上海の三十年」における記述を手がかりとして、芥川龍之介が上海を訪れた際に四六時中行動を共にしたという村田との共同生活の実態を明らかにした。そのうえで、村田の記者としての経歴や問題関心、さらに上海日本人社会における文芸文化環境の調査を通じて、芥川の会談相手として社会主義者の李人傑が選ばれた背景を検討した。加えて、村田と「支那の話、文学の話」を交わし、多くの蒙を啓かれたにもかかわらず、芥川が「上海游記」の中で専ら彼の京劇趣味に紙幅を割いたのはなぜか、という点についても考察を行った。 調査の過程で明らかになったのは、李人傑が東京大学の新人会などの左翼団体と交流を持ち、さらに上海の日本語雑誌（『上海公論』誌上に、李による中国語文章1本、日本語論説文3本が掲載されたことを新たに発見）においても対日意見を発信していたため、1920年前後にはその名が上海の日本人知識層の間で広く知られていたという事実である。加えて、1921年4月頭には、内ヶ崎作三郎が李人傑の通訳で復旦大学で講演を行い、話題となった出来事があった。こうしたことも、芥川と村田が李人傑に嘱目する契機の一つとなった可能性がある。 …

abstract: Abstract This article examines how during the 1970s, state, media, and research institutions transformed bōsōzoku – the contemporaneous label for cohorts of motorcycle-riding youth – into an object of governance. abstract: This article examines the layered meanings and evolving functions of public history in both academic scholarship and wider societal practice. It explores how the various components of public history intersect and how these entanglements reshape the conditions under which historical knowledge is produced, circulated, and authorized. As a subfield of historical studies, public history investigates representations and uses of the past, including ephemeral, embodied or performative practices that restage historical events. To research such representations public historians employ inter- and …

title: Constitutionalism of the Dispossessed: Land Occupations, Revolution, and the Political Economy of a Counter-Revolution in the Ottoman Empire
abstract: Abstract Following the proclamation of constitutionalism on 23 July 1908, villagers throughout the Ottoman Empire occupied and reclaimed çiftlik (plantation) lands from which they had previously been dispossessed. This article approaches the Ottoman 1908 Revolution as part of the “global wave of constitutional revolutions” by shifting the historiographical focus of the 1908 revolution from urban to agrarian spaces. It investigates a series of land occupations that emerged across the Ottoman çiftlik geography, conceptualizing them as the “constitutionalism of the dispossessed.” I argue that …
journal: Comparative Studies in Society and History

title: Memory Studies and History: trajectories of an academic relationship
abstract: Against the background of how interdisciplinary Memory Studies emancipated itself from academic History over the last century, we examine current research trends through a quantitative and qualitative analysis of the two main journals of the field, namely Memory Studies and History and Memory. On this basis, we discuss how the relationship between Memory Studies and History operates in the interdisciplinary practice of today’s humanities and social sciences, and what intellectual and practical challenges these encounters pose for historians.

title: Against Typical Yokosuka: Ishiuchi Miykao’s Zessho, Yokosuka Story
abstract: This article discusses Ishiuchi Miyako (1947–)’s 1979 photobook, Zesshō, Yokosuka Story as her distinctive response to images of Yokosuka produced by her mentors such as Tōmatsu Shōmei (1930–2012), Daidō Moriyama (1938–), and Tokiwa Toyoko (1928–2019). From the onset of Yokosuka project, Ishiuchi, who grew up in Yokosuka, had a strong determination to present “real” Yokosuka, distancing herself from above-noted photographers who reduced the entire city into a camptown by highlighting and typifying the presence of the American GIs, camptown sex workers, and mixed-race children. This paper …

title: Enduring Medical Knowledge in the Age of Slavery
abstract: Abstract Eighteenth- and nineteenth-century slave management texts, plantation guidebooks, medical dissertations, and treatises on preserving health in hot climates functioned as authoritative sources on the specific traits, symptoms, and health complaints of enslaved Black people. That said, information found in these texts, especially specific physiological assertions about Black people’s bodies, were not always uniform. While doctors largely agreed that Black people had a high pain tolerance and ease during childbirth, there was less consensus around the amount of therapeutic bloodletting …

title: Integration of Russian-speaking male migrants in Japan: Exploring the interplay of immigration regime, marriage, and gender
abstract: This paper examines the current state of male migrant integration in Japan. While existing research concentrates on female marital migration, the intersection of migration and marriage for men remains underexplored. Our fieldwork-based research focuses on the integration experiences of Russian-speaking men from former Soviet Union countries, who are married to Japanese women and reside in Japan. We examine aspects of men’s integration, including residential status, employment opportunities, family gender dynamics, ethnic and local affiliations, and self-identification. By exploring these at …

title: Private parties for a new world order: Maurice and Hanne Strong, global governance, and environmental imaginaries since 1970
abstract: Abstract Focusing on the private governance networks of Maurice Frederick Strong and his second wife, Hanne Marstrand, this article traces the origins of corporate environmentalism and flexible interpretations of sustainable development to the 1970s, the foundational years of international environmental governance. Shifting the analytical focus from official meetings to private gatherings in the Strongs’ homes in Geneva, Nairobi, the Canadian Rockies, and Crestone, Colorado, I show that the environmental imaginaries among governance elites around Strong and Marstrand were shaped by the …

title: Getting creative with medieval landscape fragments: the Hull Maritime Museum, late-medieval poetry, and digital availability
abstract: Abstract In this article, I reflect on my creative practice in the poetry pamphlet Exhibits from the Maritime Museum & the City, an output of my poetry residency at the Hull Maritime Museum from 2020 to 2021. Exhibits is intended as an alternative creative guide to the museum. Drawing on an established tradition of contemporary poets who ‘revoice’ medieval texts and landscapes, these poems engage with the fragmentary layered aural, textual, and environmental medieval landscapes of Hull and the Humber estuary as they are mediated through the museum and its collection of objects or artefacts. …

title: The Mandeville -author’s sense of space: a digital–ecological reading of Mandeville’s Travels
abstract: Abstract Combining digital and eco-critical analyses, this essay argues that in the Middle English version of Mandeville’s Travels, authorial emphasis on the topographical and theological centrality of Jerusalem forms the ideological keynote. Nevertheless, the overarching tendency of constructing the Holy City within the framework of composing a Christocentric universal history coincides with occasional shifts of authorial attention to the prospering civilizations in the non-Christian East (e.g. Cathay, India, and Arabia), which corresponds to some temporary and local centres of the …

title: Contact zone, desertion, or endurance? A spatial digital humanities approach to interpreting Irish medieval settlements
abstract: Abstract Following a successful pilot phase, the Human-Environmental Exchanges in the Landscapes of Medieval Ireland Project (HELM) has developed an interdisciplinary methodology to identify the location and features of heretofore thought vanished medieval settlements. This innovative methodology integrates evidence from historical accounts, archaeological fieldwork, and remote sensing data collected by Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV, or drone). Digital models created and analyzed during project workflows are used to identify the minute remnants of medieval vernacular building in the …

title: Gender, work, and mobility: Experiences of young skilled Taiwanese women in Tokyo headquarters
abstract: Over the past decade, the number of white-collar migrants employed in Japan’s corporate headquarters has increased notably. While previous research underscores the challenges Japanese firms face in attracting and retaining foreign professionals, the rapidly growing presence of skilled migrants calls for renewed attention to Japan’s continued appeal. Focusing on young, college-educated Taiwanese women, this study examines why they move from a society ranked as having higher gender equality to one ranked with lower gender equality, and how they navigate their careers within Japan’s gendered …

title: ‘Inside the belly of the monster’: The politics of race in Britain, transnational anti-colonialism, and the Black Liberation Front
abstract: Abstract This article examines anti-colonialism and Third World solidarities in Britain during the 1970s and 1980s. It does so through a study of the Black Liberation Front (BLF), a Black Power group formed in London in 1971. The BLF saw themselves as part of a global Third World solidarity, and, as activists in Britain, identified their location as ‘inside the belly of the monster’. They understood racism and colonialism as global phenomena, and offered material support to anti-colonial movements across the world, especially in Africa. The prevailing historiography of Black activism in …

title: Coextension of knowledge networks and technological infrastructures: The Jesuits and meteorology in late colonial Asia
abstract: Abstract This article challenges the traditional view of the linear causality of technological globalization in the history of modern predictive meteorology. According to this linear narrative, telegraphy, by enabling near-instantaneous communication over vast distances, was the causa efficiens that directly and inevitably produced large-scale weather forecasting. However, the role of Jesuit scientists in East Asia as pioneers of cyclone warning systems not only demonstrates that the linear narrative is too simple but invites a rigorous examination of the relationships between prior knowledge …

title: Medicine, Race, and Slavery in the Transatlantic World, 1600–1850
abstract: As the title suggests, the provocation of this Supplement is simple: that the histories of medicine, transatlantic slavery, and race cannot, and should not, be viewed separately. Between 1440 and 1888 more than twelve million African people were forcibly trafficked across the Atlantic Ocean, enslaved in plantations, cities, and homes across the Americas, the Caribbean, and Europe.1 We are used to thinking about this as a ‘triangle’, in which the flows were raw materials and trafficked individuals, and the static points geographic sites.2 Imagine instead a triangle where the points are …

title: Water’s Worth: Reconsidering Deutsche Bank’s 1907 Konya Plain Irrigation Project
abstract: The 1907 Konya Plain Irrigation Project redefined local ecologies and catalysed material and political changes in central Anatolia. Often overshadowed by the Anatolian Railway Company’s railway infrastructure, this study highlights Deutsche Bank’s pivotal role in environmental engineering. As the Ottoman Empire relied on foreign capital for infrastructural projects, the Konya Project emerged as a nexus of state centralisation and capitalist enterprise, reshaping Anatolia’s agricultural landscape. The project aimed to create a rationally planned, mechanised and export-oriented agricultural …

title: Bombay Cyclones: An Environmental History of the West Coast of India in the Eighteenth and Nineteenth Centuries
abstract: While Bombay’s rains have always been an intriguing research topic, the cyclones faced by the city and its surroundings have not received much attention. The study of tropical cyclones on the east coast of the Indian subcontinent, especially those that struck the coastal regions of present-day Bangladesh, has been a focus of many environmental historians. However, the question remains whether Bombay and its surroundings were less affected in this regard. In this paper, thorough research has been conducted on the cyclones that hit the West Coast, especially Bombay, using both official sources …

title: Multifunctional Landscapes in Central Mainland Portugal: The Royal Administration of Almeirim and Sustainable Land Use from the Fourteenth to the Sixteenth Century
abstract: This article addresses two hundred years of administration and land use around Almeirim, a city located on the left bank of the River Tagus near Santarém. Through legislation and other administrative documents, it reconstructs the historical progression of different kinds of land use and generates maps showing the approximate limits of the spatial scope of regulation. Three main conclusions may be drawn: first, the dynamics of the royal forests of Almeirim cannot be understood without considering the dynamics of the surrounding areas; second, the Portuguese Crown sought to conserve resources …

title: Digital objects as translation: their digitization depth as a taxonomy for digital analogues
abstract: Abstract Digital collections of historical objects are increasingly the first interface when setting up new academic enquiries in the Humanities. This influences how research questions are formed. The size of these collections is posited to grow even more as the costs of digitization decrease and access widens. Framing digital collections and their contents correctly is therefore of great importance. However, in many cases the conceptualization of digitized collections remains in practice tied to the mistaken notion that digital copies are surrogates for the analogue originals they represent, …

title: The Japanese Morphine Industry, 1880s to 1940s
abstract: Abstract Historians have explored Japanese drug manufacture and trafficking in Asia in the first half of the twentieth century. They have pointed out that in the same decades a domestically oriented morphine industry developed as result of Japanese efforts to achieve self-sufficiency. However, little attention has been paid to the development and impact of this industry. This article argues that the Japanese morphine industry had a significant impact on Japanese agriculture, promoted the rationalization of production processes in factories, and stood for a modern medical consumer culture. It …

title: CONFISCATION AS GOVERNANCE IN THE OTTOMAN EMPIRE, 1750–1839
abstract: Abstract Müsadere, the confiscation of the estates of dismissed or deceased officials in the Ottoman Empire, has been viewed as a marker of despotism, an impediment to capitalism, a legitimate form of punishment, and a useful fiscal and political instrument. However, beyond case studies, the empire-wide logic and dynamics behind this practice remain elusive. Using both qualitative evidence and a rich dataset of confiscation attempts informed by a historically-informed interpretative scheme, this article examines the dynamics that shaped the enforcement of müsadere and their broader …

title: Special issue—Digital Humanities 2023: Collaboration as Opportunity
abstract: The 2023 edition of ADHO’s annual global conference ‘Digital Humanities’ took place in Graz under the theme of ‘Collaboration as Opportunity’. DH2023 showcased transdisciplinary and transnational collaboration, with a special focus on the thriving South-Eastern European Digital Humanities community. It explored how mutual empowerment and collaboration of neighbouring countries—regardless of continent and geopolitical placement—can transform regional hubs of expertise into international networks of excellent research, to the benefit of the global DH community. title: The Icelander in the Angloworld: Race and rethinking world order in the fin de siècle North
abstract: Abstract This article recovers the international thought of Jón Ólafsson—an Icelandic journalist, transatlantic migrant, and settler colonialist—to illuminate how visions of world order were articulated from the Northern European periphery at the fin de siècle . While scholars have emphasized the rise of Anglo-Saxonist ideas—particularly the notion of a racial-imperial union between the United States and Britain—as central to late nineteenth-century reimaginings of global politics, little attention has been paid to how such ideas were adapted beyond the English-speaking world itself. Tracing …

title: Discipline and subversion: emotional labor and career development of highly skilled Chinese women in Japan
abstract: This study investigates the career development and emotional labor processes of highly skilled Chinese women in Japanese corporations, uncovering how intersecting forces of cultural difference, gendered discipline, and occupational hierarchy shape their professional trajectories. Through in-depth qualitative interviews with 35 highly skilled Chinese women working in Tokyo, this study examines how highly skilled migrant women navigate emotional labor through concealed resistance and resilience in cross-cultural workplaces. They strategically employ adaptive tactics, cultivate personal …

title: HISTORICAL REALITY: A MANIFESTO
abstract: ABSTRACT From the times of Herodotus and Thucydides until deep into the eighteenth century, the eyewitness account (or “autopsy”) was the model for historical knowledge. The eighteenth‐century Historical Revolution replaced this emphasis on autopsy by introducing the notion of the point of view, as explicated in Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz's Monadology . That notion radically separated the historian's present from the world of the eyewitness's past. title: The Fugitive Steppe: Climate and Colonialism on the Kazakh Steppe, 1860–1916
abstract: This article examines how Russian imperial ambitions to transform the Kazakh steppe between 1840 and 1914 were shaped by and in turn reshaped understandings of climate. As Russian scientists and administrators encountered Central Asia’s continental climate, with its extremes of heat and cold, they developed theories that recast the steppe’s aridity from an immutable natural barrier into a condition that could be ‘improved’ through European cultivation and settlement. It reveals how environmental theories became instruments of empire. The resulting transformations not only made Kazakhs …

title: Squid and Socialists: Power, Nature and the Unruly East Sea in North Korea, 1945–1964
abstract: Squid – ten-limbed cephalopods with lifespans of only a year and migratory habits – reveal a maritime history of North Korea defined by volatility and frustration. This paper reconstructs how squid in the East Sea undermined production quotas and eluded state planning from 1945 to 1964, showing how nonhuman herd agency exposed the limits of Pyongyang’s efforts to discipline oceanic nature. Briefly celebrated in propaganda as symbols of abundance in the early 1960s, squid soon revealed the fragility of postcolonial ambition and Soviet-style development. Drawing on underused Korean and Soviet …

title: Reshaping Perception: Chiang Kai-shek's Preliminary Approach to the Soviet Union, 1934–5
abstract: This article offers a new perspective on Sino–Soviet relations in the mid-1930s by examining how Chiang Kai-shek strategically reshaped Soviet perceptions of his political stance. Against the background that the Nanjing government was pursuing rapprochement with Japan, Chiang recast himself in Soviet eyes from a pro-Japanese leader to a potential anti-Japanese ally. He achieved this by exploiting the fragmented appearance of authority within the Nanjing government, distancing himself from the conciliatory policies towards Japan, and aligning with Soviet interests on key issues such as …

title: Beyond the Cold War and decolonization: Nigerian foreign policy, French nuclear tests, and the politics of independence in West Africa
abstract: Abstract As the first foreign policy issue Nigeria debated, the controversy around France’s nuclear tests, conducted in Algeria during the War of Independence there, allowed Lagos to rehearse its envisioned African role even before formal independence in October 1960. Nigerian opposition to France eventually culminated in the expulsion of the French ambassador on 5 January 1961, after the third French atomic test in the Algerian Sahara. This seemingly straightforward anti-colonial and anti-nuclear act was in fact largely driven by inter-African dynamics, particularly Nigeria’s complicated …

title: Buffalo Politics: Sovereignty and Sacrificial Publics in the Highlands of East India
abstract: Abstract Public rituals of buffalo sacrifice have a prominent place in the political history of eastern India. They were productive activities in agrarian livelihoods, stages for intercommunal politics, unifying spectacles for regional kings, and justifications for colonial military interventions. While their historical scale is much reduced today, in parts of southern Odisha, they remain important political events. Drawing on historical research and long-term ethnographic fieldwork in Odisha’s Kandhamal Hills, this article examines how public rituals of sacrifice form a site of …

title: The visual construction of Vasily Eroshenko’s image in China: Media, memory, and “loneliness” through Chu Baoheng’s photography
abstract: Abstract This study examines how the blind Russian poet Vasily Eroshenko (1890–1952) was visually constructed in 1920s China through Chu Baoheng’s photography, transforming him from political exile to transcultural icon during the May Fourth Movement (1919–1924). Through formal visual analysis of six key photographs taken between 1921 and 1923, this research reveals how these images functioned simultaneously as documentary evidence, cultural allegory, and philosophical “metapictures” – images that reflect on the process of pictorial representation itself. title: A commoning framework for environmental archaeology: beyond resource management in Indigenous North America
abstract: Environmental archaeology has often relied on common-pool resource models to interpret past human-environment relationships, yet these frameworks overlook Indigenous ontologies grounded in kinship with land, water, and more-than human beings. We propose commoning as a complementary approach that centers reciprocity, relational care, and cultural meaning alongside institutional regulation. Drawing on archaeological evidence from Virginia's Chesapeake Bay, we show how commoning reveals Indigenous environmental governance as a world-making practice. This framework advances environmental …

title: Medical Practitioners, The Archive, and the Making of Slavery in Early Modern Barbados
abstract: Abstract In seventeenth-century Barbados medical practitioners abounded, frequently operated as planters and merchants, and amassed sizeable estates. Their wills and property deeds attest to the efficacy of their professional ambitions and their important role in the formation of colonial Barbadian society. They also testify, unambiguously, to the frequency with which medical practitioners owned enslaved individuals, whose names were as prominent and more numerous in medical wills than were the names of wives, children, siblings, and friends. title: “Fattening” One Health: An Interspecies Approach to Dismantling the “Obesity Epidemic”
abstract: Abstract The past 30 years have been marked by the alleged public health threat of the human “obesity epidemic” and recently parallel concerns have surfaced regarding “obesity” in companion animals. Simultaneously, new research has questioned not only rising “obesity” rates but also weight as a reliable determinant of human health and it is becoming apparent that the medicalization and stigmatization of fatness have a profound effect on patients’ quality of medical care. Moreover, fat studies scholars have offered a critical perspective on how fatphobia is institutionalized within our medical …

title: O historiador com SIAPE
abstract: A relação entre Teoria da História e o ensino de história tem sido cada vez mais enfatizada nos últimos anos. Parte dessas contribuições aborda a relação entre o campo da Teoria e a prática da sala de aula no Ensino Superior, destacando a necessidade de uma escuta ativa, da reavaliação dos conteúdos ensinados e da proposição de atividades pedagógicas que contemplem uma sala de aula que, afirma-se, é substantivamente diferente daquela de alguns anos atrás. title: From holy prince to legal ancestor: Shōtoku in Japan’s modern constitutional imagination
abstract: This article examines one strand in the modern development of the image of Prince Shōtoku (Shōtoku Taishi, 574–622), the semi-mythical statesman portrayed in the Nihon shoki as an ideal ‘sagely king’. While Shōtoku-related lore has been repeatedly reimagined, the twentieth century saw a decisive shift to a secularized image that presented him as a lay Buddhist exemplar, pioneer of diplomacy, champion of meritocracy, and architect of constitutional governance. Focusing on this last dimension, this article begins with recent examples from politics, education, and popular media that depict …

title: The Rohingya and Arakan
abstract: Abstract Using this forum's political economy and political ecology framework, this lead article reexamines the process of identifying the Rohingya as “foreign” to Arakan as one rooted in the region's uneven development. Conflicts that the British colonial state conceptualized as primarily “communal”—such as, in this case, the conflict between Rakhines, Rohingya, and Indians in Arakan—more accurately reflected a struggle to capture land and resources on the margins of empire, where economic planning was particularly privatized and uneven. abstract: This article examines how Murayama Tomoyoshi’s proletarian theater engaged with the socialist revolutionary movement in Republican China (1912–1949) to articulate proletarian solidarity between the Chinese and Japanese working-class and critique Japanese imperialism. title: Free ports, political economy, and early globalization: Evidence from 1750s Hamburg
abstract: Abstract Recent scholarship locates the origins of modern free trade policies in the early modern free port movement. This historiography has focused on the intellectual and political history of free ports and emphasized the importance of local and regional factors in shaping trade liberalizations in different European countries and colonies. Based on evidence from eighteenth-century Hamburg, this article proposes a different reading: it argues that free trade policies emerged in response to Atlantic trade expansion. abstract: Two non-humans from Old Norse mythology have achieved a popularity that eclipses some of the deities in the pantheon: corvids Huginn and Muninn. In pre-Christian Iron Age beliefs, Huginn and Muninn were the shrewd ravens of Óðinn, Allfather, the supreme god of the Æsir, the gods of the Old Norse tradition. These two ravens perched on Óðinn’s shoulders, and their names indicate that they represented thought (Huginn) and memory (Muninn). title: A Critical Collection History of Nineteenth-century Women’s Letters: Overcoming the Occluded Archive with Data-Driven Methods
abstract: This paper presents a virtual archive of women’s epistolary exchange in 19th-century Finland. By harmonising metadata from over 1.2 million letters and over 100,000 correspondents across key cultural heritage organisations and leveraging linked open data, we gain an unprecedented view of 19th-century epistolary communication and 20th-century archival practices. Using quantitative analysis, enriched metadata, and network visualisations, we explore the gendered nature of these collections. Are women archival protagonists, or are their materials embedded within the collections of male relatives? …

title: Evaluating and Understanding the Geocoding of City Directories of Paris (1787-1914): Data-Driven Geography of Urban Sprawl and Densification
abstract: As in other western cities, the fast-paced urban, industrial, and commercial sprawl of Paris during the 19th century provided the backdrop and driving force for the publishing phenomenon of trade directories. We show how these collections of millions of nominative entries associated with addresses can be turned into a serial dataset whose massive, fine-grained, and geolocated nature opens up new possibilities for quantitative and multi-scale analyses of the dynamics at play during one of the most dramatic socio-spatial transformations of the city. We highlight the methodological conditions of …

title: Making Sense of the Emergence of Manslaughter in British Criminal Justice
abstract: Manslaughter emerged as a new and distinct category of crime amongst those tried at the Old Bailey in London in the first half of the nineteenth century. From being a rare charge in 1800, manslaughter came to represent over 60% of all trials for ‘killing’ by the 1850s. This article describes the methodologies used by the authors to explore this phenomenon via trials included in the Old Bailey Online. It details the use of unsupervised clustering, embeddings and relevance measures to map the changing language associated with the charge of manslaughter; and more importantly, describes the …

title: Assemblies of Points: Strategies to Art-historical Human Pose Estimation and Retrieval
abstract: This paper attempts to construct a virtual space of possibilities for the historical embedding of the human figure, and its posture, in the visual arts by proposing a view-invariant approach to Human Pose Retrieval (HPR) that resolves the ambiguity of projecting three-dimensional postures onto their two-dimensional counterparts. In addition, we present a refined approach for classifying human postures using a support set of 110 art-historical reference postures. The method’s effectiveness on art-historical images was validated through a two-stage approach of broad-scale filtering preceded by …

title: Image Reuse in Eighteenth-Century Book History: Large-Scale Data-Driven Study of Headpiece Ornament Variants
abstract: This study uses large-scale computational analysis to trace the reuse of decorative headpieces in eighteenth-century books. The results highlight how image variants reveal complex networks of printers and publishers beyond simple one-to-one ownership.

title: Introduction: History and Data Science: Data-driven Inquiries into the Past
abstract: The integration of data science methods into historical research is an emerging joint focus of digital humanities and history. This new research area applies data science methods to study large historical datasets, such as correspondences, chronicles, oral history interviews, photos, and maps. As part of the overarching goal to further our knowledge of the past, the application of data science methods in historical research involves an array of epistemological questions as well. For instance, what can count as evidence and knowledge in the context of data driven inquiries into the past?

title: Advocating for inclusive narratives: A call for critical engagement with the palm oil agribusiness sector
abstract: The palm oil industry, a significant economic driver in South-east Asia, remains at the centre of intense global scrutiny due to environmental and human rights concerns persist. Despite its high productivity per hectare, critics continue to raise concerns about its role in deforestation, biodiversity loss and exploitative labour practices. The industry’s transnational nature further complicates these debates, shaping public perception and policy discourse. Overwhelmingly, the narrative about this sector focuses on negative consequences, warning consumers of importing deforestation and …

title: The king’s word: Colonial contracting and financial capitalism in Moskitia during the scramble for Central America, 1824–42
abstract: Abstract This article examines how Miskitu King Robert Charles Frederic (1824–42) used colonial contracts with foreign merchants to advance his political agenda in Moskitia, on Central America’s Caribbean coast. Drawing on European and Central American archives, this study challenges narratives that portray Indigenous leaders as passive actors in colonial expansion, highlighting how the king strategically wielded contracts to facilitate the import of foreign capital through concessions and loans. His mastery of international finance enabled resistance to imperial domination while allowing him …

title: Cod and its oil, cuisine and its supplements: Fish fragmentation, commodity connections and naturalising resources in Newfoundland
abstract: By spotlighting cod liver oil as an example of a global fat and reflecting on the commercialisation of fish – from food source and medicine to dietary supplement – this article surveys cod’s colonial history in Newfoundland alongside cultural imaginations of resources. The oil’s popularity boomed in the early twentieth century with the discovery of vitamins, which gifted foods and their by-products new values. This article thus sketches out how fish, fat and commercial markets connect the history of cod liver oil in Newfoundland with the world. Prioritising three cultural artefacts – a folk …

title: Meanings of sustainability: The invention of sustainable palm oil
abstract: Palm oil production started in the early twentieth century and expanded tremendously from the 1970s, with the area of palm oil plantations in Malaysia alone increasing by a factor of 74 between 1975 and 2010, causing significant tropical deforestation, carbon emissions and loss of biodiversity. This article examines meanings of sustainability in the history of palm oil production and in the recent efforts of the Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil (RSPO). Based on sustainability and postcolonial scholarship, and drawing on the examples of the Danish plantation company United Plantations in …

title: Autarkic, but global: Fat supply and whaling in pre-war Nazi Germany
abstract: Nazi Germany started whaling in the Antarctic Ocean in 1936 as a result of its high dependence on fat imports and a shortage of foreign currency. While this was part of a policy geared towards self-sufficiency or autarky, whaling did not cut Germany off from the international links that characterise the global fat supply, but actually created new connections. The article sets out four new arguments. First, Germany never achieved self-sufficiency in whale oil or fat in general. Second, in the context of whaling, links to Norway remained strong. Third, the Anglo-Dutch Unilever group was a key …

title: Food chemistry, fat experiment and palm oil in late Soviet politics and industry
abstract: This article discusses the development of food chemistry in the Soviet Union beginning in the late 1950s. It analyses how, amid a growing cult of chemistry, scientists sought to address food crises and envisioned the creation of modern, scientifically engineered food. This study examines the scientific beliefs and experiments as well as their political relevance in response to persistent food shortage. Emphasising the fact that these experiments were successful in the laboratories but limited in industrial production, the article examines initiatives such as synthesising food – the project …

title: Whaling as an interim oil supply industry: The rise and fall of whale oil in the competitive fat and oil markets
abstract: Whale oil, a general term for products derived from the fats and oils of numerous cetacean species, is a global resource whose purveyors have historically been buffeted by economic, technological, and environmental forces. It remained a viable international commodity in the first half of the twentieth century due to a remarkable shift from its use mainly for lighting and lubrication to one used for food products such as margarine and even explosives, before it quickly faded as alternatives emerged and environmental regulations took hold. While previous studies have illuminated various aspects …

title: From communal agropastoral practices to the slaughterhouses in the Brazilian border line with Argentina: the significance of lard in settlers’ narratives (1930s–1960s)
abstract: This article addresses how, between the 1920s and 1960s, the Brazilian border line with Argentina, a territory then known as a ‘demographic vacuum’, received a considerable number of migrants from the neighbouring state of Rio Grande do Sul, with the intention of establishing an occupation through colonisation. Specifically, this paper explores how the settlers capitalised on an existing agricultural and pastoral production model to set up small butcher’s shops and establish a market based on lard that became integrated into other regions in the following decades. With the purpose of …

title: Fat: Lubricant of modernity
abstract: This article explores the global history of fat as both a vital nutrient and a versatile industrial commodity from the nineteenth to early twentieth centuries. The study highlights fat’s expanding applications – from foodstuffs like margarine and shortening to non-food products including soaps, paints and early plastics. Drawing on historical data and trade patterns, it reveals how colonial and geopolitical dynamics shaped resource preferences. The article calls for situating fat within broader narratives of industrialisation, globalisation, and imperialism and integrating it into commodity …

title: Global entanglements of palm oil and kernel extraction from French West Africa (c. 1840–1960)
abstract: This article links the regional history of palm oil and kernel extraction in French West Africa to the global history of fat resources. It argues that what happened to fat resources produced and consumed elsewhere is crucial to understanding how the extraction of West African palm products developed over time. The article illustrates how the French became interested in West African palm oil in the nineteenth century in their search for fats for soap production, and how the colonial conquest of the region was linked to the West African groundnut crisis. In the twentieth century, the way in …

title: Fish oil’s journey through Russian and Soviet history
abstract: Throughout Russian, Soviet and post-Soviet eras, fish oil has repeatedly changed its role as scientific and technological advances rendered earlier uses obsolete. Originally prized by coastal communities as a dense caloric supplement, it evolved into a cornerstone source of vitamins A and D and later achieved prominence through its rich omega-3 profile, after these fatty acids were recognised for health. In Soviet times, fish oil transcended its nutritional and medicinal roles to become a tool of state health policy and a miraculous lifeline, in particular during the Siege of Leningrad. …

title: Roots and dynamics of Dutch foreign plant-oil demands 1920–2020
abstract: Dutch harbours became key notes in European foreign fat supply in the twentieth century. These imports of oils and fats have had significant economic, social and environmental impacts worldwide. This paper investigates the development of Dutch imports of oils and fats over the past century. title: Mobility without Diaspora: Japan’s Return-Oriented National Imaginary in the Age of Transnationalism
abstract: Despite its global cultural reach and economic power, Japan remains an anomalous case among major states in its limited outward migration and absence of a politically or economically mobilised diaspora. This article conceptualises Japan as a non-diasporic nation, arguing that its demographic inwardness reflects deeper civilisational logics shaped by post-imperial retrenchment, ethnonationalist identity, and institutional frameworks privileging repatriation over dispersion. title: Only Human: Occupation Censorship of ‘Imperial Myths’ In Japanese Textbooks
abstract: This paper examines Occupation-era censorship policies, focusing on the portrayal of the divinity of the emperor and the inclusion of imperial myths in Japanese textbooks. It reveals that the concept of the emperor as a ‘living god’ (akitsumikami) only appeared in textbooks starting in 1940. Beyond showing the limitations and bluntness of these censorship efforts, the analysis highlights how Occupation authorities leveraged the emperor’s image to justify their reforms. title: Sob os tempos do equinócio: oito mil anos de história na Amazônia Central
abstract: RésuméPartout en Amazonie, on trouve des villes et des zones urbaines comparées à Venise. Cet essai explore les origines de cette comparaison évocatrice, en se concentrant sur la ville brésilienne de Manaus pendant le boom du caoutchouc de la fin du xixe et du début du xxe siècle. En s’appuyant sur l’analyse des systèmes mondiaux et de l’écologie mondiale, il soutient que l’archétype de la « Venise de la jungle » peut mettre en lumière des schémas, mais aussi des divergences et des changements, dans les modes d’organisation de la nature à travers les espaces géographiques et au fil du temps.

title: Extracting ideological dimensions from legislative speeches in the Japanese Diet
abstract: Abstract Understanding the ideological positions of political parties is crucial for empirically testing various theories in political science. In Japan, some studies have assessed each party’s policy outlook through electoral platforms, candidate surveys, or expert surveys, with most studies focusing on the past thirty years. However, limited efforts have comprehensively and longitudinally quantified the conflicts between political parties. title: Limited lifelines: International Friendship Associations bridging COVID-19 support gaps in peri-urban Japan
abstract: Abstract This Research Note analyses how volunteer-run International Friendship Associations (IFAs) in peri-urban Ibaraki bridged gaps in migrant support during the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic. Fieldwork in Kōga and Toride combined twenty semi-structured interviews with IFA officers and volunteers, migrant residents (Specified Skilled Worker [SSW], long-term, family, naturalized), and municipal liaisons, with participant observation and organizational records. Routine activities became crisis infrastructure. IFAs performed three linked functions: language access, which …

title: World Federalism in the Early Postwar Thought of Kagawa Toyohiko
abstract: This paper examines Christian socialist Kagawa Toyohiko, with a focus on his evolving ideas about world federalism. From his involvement with cooperatives in the Taisho period until his advocacy of world federalism immediately after World War II, Kagawa sought alternatives to capitalist society and the Westphalian system of international relations. After World War II, his support for Japan as the center of an Asian federation was, in certain ways, enigmatic given Japan’s recent past in Asia during the war.

abstract: This essay examines attempts between 1920 and 1945 to tackle “examination hell,” meaning the pressures on children that resulted from competition to enter secondary school. Debates about “examination hell” centered on harm to children, to education, and ultimately to the nation. Arguments weighed issues of fair competition between individuals, alongside the needs of the state. From 1939, reforms to secondary entrance procedures manifested radical statism, in parallel with extensions of state control in other areas of national life. title: Relapse into Barbarism? Explaining the Port Arthur Massacre, November 1894
abstract: Between November 21 and 24, 1894, during the First Sino-Japanese War, Imperial Japanese forces perpetrated a large-scale massacre in Port Arthur, a strategic port in southern Manchuria. This event, relatively understudied in English-language historiography, ran contrary to the Imperial Army’s policy and undermined Japan’s concurrent initiatives to secure Western recognition as a “civilized state.” Moreover, the massacre was an anomaly, considering the generally restrained conduct of the Imperial Japanese Army toward Chinese civilians and POWs during that war. abstract: Sakata Kiyoko’s 2016 poem-video installation Taigan ni tsuite (About Opposite Shores) transforms excerpts of Zainichi Korean poet Kim Si-jong’s 1970 narrative poem Niigata into a performative artwork consisting of words and salt crystals distilled from seawater. title: Palace of Time
abstract: Analyzing the ongoing reconstruction of monumental buildings from the long-lost imperial palace in Nara, this article argues that the symbolic significance of the historic site finds expression in three temporal aspects: past, present, and future. Approaching historical reconstruction as symbolic stabilization of national time and spatial order, the article analyzes claimed interconnections between material structures and abstract qualities under all three temporal horizons. Arguing that the site’s symbolic importance brings together diverse stakeholder interests, this article adds new …

title: Making Room to Grow
abstract: This paper examines rōnin (“masterless samurai”) and the rōnin label in Tokugawa Japan (1603–1868) through a focus on their interactions with rural areas and rural development projects. By positioning rōnin as a highly varied social group in search of livelihood and social status, this paper shows that conventional descriptions of them as disruptive ruffians overlook their social significance and complexities and misunderstand their existence as rural semi-elite. It highlights that rōnin were an important factor in the expansion of rural productivity, and that the rōnin label was instrumental …

title: Not just unequal, but unfair? Perceived economic inequality, regional disparities, and party support in Japan
abstract: Abstract Japan has long been portrayed as a relatively egalitarian society. Yet, growing economic disparities have raised questions about how inequality is perceived and politicized. This study examines whether regional economic inequality shapes individuals’ perceptions of rich–poor conflict and how such perceptions translate into political preferences. Using individual-level data from the SmartNews, Media, Politics, and Public Opinion Survey (SMPP Survey) combined with prefectural indicators of inequality, income, and unemployment, the analysis adopts a multilevel framework to link …

title: Residential inequality and social class perceptions: a case study of the Tokyo metropolitan area
abstract: This study investigates how inequalities in the Tokyo metropolitan area shape residents’ perceptions of social class. I focus on two aspects of social class perceptions: images of social structure (ISS) and subjective social status (SSS). Given that these two aspects are direct perceptions of social structure, the rapid increase in income inequality and polarization that have developed in the Tokyo area in recent years may have significantly affected ISS and SSS. However, the relationship has not yet been fully examined. Using data from the Tokyo Metropolitan Area Residents 2016 survey, the …

In 1880, Keio, a private school in Japan, was at risk of closure. To address this, the school launched a fundraising campaign in the 1880–90 period. Established in 1857, the school has distributed a list covering all students’ academic records to teachers and students since 1861. title: Neighborhood participation and foreign resident life satisfaction in Japan
abstract: Abstract Research on immigrant life satisfaction rarely examines Japan’s rapidly expanding foreign population. Applying social production function theory, we examine how neighborhood participation influences life satisfaction among foreign nationals in Nagoya. Using ordered logit regression analysis of survey data from 1,496 foreign residents collected in 2015, we test effects of four participation forms: social contact with Japanese neighbors, membership in neighborhood household associations (NHAs), volunteering, and event participation. title: The price premium for a Tokyo Tower view: evidence from quantile difference-in-differences analysis during COVID-19 pandemic
abstract: Abstract This study investigates whether Tokyo Tower’s visibility premium persisted around the coronavirus disease 2019 shock. By measuring Tower views using three-dimensional geographic analysis in ArcGIS Pro, this hedonic study applies a quantile difference-in-differences model using online condominium sales (2017–22) in seven Tokyo wards to compare pandemic-era price appreciation for residential units with and without a Tower view. title: Norms for apolitical celebrities?
abstract: Abstract The purpose of this study is to identify factors that determine negative reactions to political comments by celebrities in Japan. In a democratic society, celebrities can serve an important function as intermediaries through whom large numbers of people can encounter diverse points of view. The prevailing atmosphere in Japan has little tolerance for political comments by celebrities, however, as exhibited by the commonly heard assertion that entertainers should not talk about politics. title: Do effort cues improve voter evaluations of politicians? Evidence from Japan
abstract: Abstract What factors determine voters’ evaluations of politicians? Previous studies have focused on two categories—policy-based and non-policy factors. However, they have overlooked politicians’ displays of effort as a non-policy factor, a trait that garnered considerable media attention during recent crises in Japan. Following the Great East Japan Earthquake and during the COVID-2019 pandemic, news outlets frequently showed footage of political leaders working hard to manage the crisis response. title: Rites of precarity: migrant labour and bounded inclusion in Japan’s peri-urban markets
abstract: Abstract This article examines how Japan’s labour-migration frameworks admit foreign workers while leaving many to manage persistent insecurity through the conditions attached to lawful residence. Based on ethnographic fieldwork in Ibaraki Prefecture, this study develops the concept of bounded precarity to describe a form of authorized presence in which constrained mobility, income volatility, and uneven access to protection coexist with legal recognition. Focusing on peri-urban labour markets, the article demonstrates how dispersed workplaces, seasonal work rhythms, and fragmented support …

title: The post-study abroad experience in Japan: student reintegration as future global human resources
abstract: Abstract The cultivation of global jinzai, or ‘global human resources’ (GHR), has become a key goal of Japanese higher education, and student mobility programs have been widely promoted as a way to foster the skills deemed desirable in Japanese GHR. Research suggests that study abroad may impact the career trajectory of students in Japan, but little is known about the experiences of student returnees and how their skills as GHR are cultivated, appraised, and utilized in a domestic setting post-study abroad. This article presents the results of a qualitative study designed to investigate the …

title: Analysis of flipped classrooms and learning outcomes during the COVID-19 pandemic
abstract: Abstract A flipped classroom lets students watch a video lecture before class and work on practice problems during class, which “flips” the timing of traditional lectures. This study estimates the differences in learning outcomes between flipped classrooms and traditional lectures in an introductory economics course at one university during the COVID-19 pandemic. We find suggestive evidence that in the short run flipped classrooms have negative effects on students’ learning outcomes in the in-person format while positive effects in the online format.

title: Acting Like Female Spirit Mediums
abstract: In 1913, Nakachi Kamado called for a public trial in Naha, Okinawa, to contest the accusation that she had acted as a yuta, or female spirit medium. The trial captivated city residents, drawing hundreds to the courtroom and even more to commercial theaters featuring plays about the trial. This article argues that the trial and plays articulated tensions of class and gender pulsating through the city of Naha. From police surveillance to the dispossession of the former ruling class and an influx of working-class women, tensions wrought by Japanese colonialism and urbanization found powerful …

title: The Hearts of People in the World
abstract: This article explores the economic dimensions of the late fiction of the seventeenth-century writer Ihara Saikaku, asking how the author’s understanding of the marketplace shaped his humanistic studies of “the hearts of people” (hito-gokoro). Applying methods of economic criticism to the posthumous Tying Off Saikaku’s Loose Ends (Saikaku oridome, 1694), I argue that the author’s late writings develop a formal homology between the imperfect rationality of the early market economy and the ineffable dynamism of the human heart.

title: A Businesswoman in Meiji Japan
abstract: Women are conspicuously underexamined in the business and economic histories of modern Japan. Although wives and widows played central roles in the financial management of their families and family businesses, they have typically remained hidden behind the names and accomplishments of their more visible male relations. This was true not only in Japan but also in other countries undergoing rapid industrialization in the long nineteenth century. Some women, however, did leave traces of their economic activity and leadership. As scholars encounter more and more of these so-called anomalies, the …

title: Grounding Empire Through Burial Grounds
abstract: This article examines how the Japanese military, notably the Kwantung Army, used the acquisition and maintenance of military burial grounds to challenge Chinese sovereignty in Manchuria (currently Northeast China) and expand Japan’s territorial control in seemingly “peaceful” periods. The burial grounds became contested sites where debates over sovereignty and different groups’ claims of land use played out. With a close focus on the military-use land, this article challenges the previous depiction of Japanese imperialism in Manchuria as informal imperialism and enriches our understanding of …

title: To the Virtuous Go the Spoils
abstract: This article examines Taiheiki (Chronicle of Great Peace, fourteenth century) as a critical intervention in medieval Japanese historiography. It challenges conventional court-versus-rebel binaries, framing the fragmentation of authority during the Nanbokuchō age through Neo-Confucian concepts of virtue, such as the three bonds and five virtues, the Mandate of Heaven, and revolutionary reign change. title: Ainu Handicrafts
abstract: This article examines the mass commercialization of Ainu handicrafts as Hokkaido’s official folk art and signature souvenir during the 1930s. Focusing on the political economy of these works, it analyzes how the Japanese empire constructed a colonial handicraft industry that promoted the popular consumption of Ainu woodcarvings and attus textiles as symbols of Japan’s civilizing mission over the Ainu people. title: The Breath of Nonduality: Genjū Zen, Buddhist Doctrines of Breathing, and Kōan Commentaries in Premodern Japan
abstract: Abstract: This article examines the integration of discourses on respiration into kōan exegesis within the Genjū lineage of Rinzai Zen in medieval Japan. Drawing on missan (records of private face-to-face exchanges between masters and students on various kōan ) preserved at the Matsugaoka Bunko and presenting a selection of these as annotated translations, it argues that Genjū monks developed a distinctive interpretive framework within kōan discourse in which breath occupied a central role. This framework, however, can only be fully understood when situated within broader medieval Japanese …

title: Localized Stone Forms and Local Agency: Satsuma Stupas and the Material Practice of Zen Buddhism in Kamakura Kyushu
abstract: Abstract: This article examines the Satsuma stupas ( satsumatō ), a group of distinctive stone monuments produced in coastal Kyushu during the Kamakura period, as evidence of localized Buddhist material practice shaped through transregional contact. Rather than treating these monuments as anomalous derivatives of continental prototypes or as passive by-products of maritime trade, this study approaches them as material responses to changing religious and social conditions in thirteenth-century Japan. Through a comparative analysis of stone stupa forms from Southern Song coastal China and their …

title: Institutionalized expertise and strategic deferral: explaining Japan’s delayed response to declining fertility
abstract: Abstract This article explains Japan’s delayed policy response to declining fertility by examining how institutionalized expertise shaped population governance in the post-war period. Existing studies emphasize weak problem recognition, taboos surrounding state-led population policy, and agenda-setting dynamics, but they rarely examine how these factors interacted within institutional settings. To address this gap, the article develops an analytical framework linking institutions, ideas, and behaviour that clarifies how expert interpretations translated into policy action within Japan’s …

title: New life paths among younger Japanese adults? International student mobility and gender differences in labour market outcomes and life satisfaction
abstract: Abstract As transnational human capital gains importance in Japan’s globalizing economy, international student mobility (ISM) is widely promoted as a means of improving career prospects. Yet, existing research has focused predominantly on economic returns, largely neglecting broader individual outcomes and gender inequalities. This study examines the associations between ISM, labour market outcomes, and life satisfaction among Japan’s post-ice-age generation, i.e. cohorts entering the labour market after 2004. Using longitudinal data from the SSJDA Panel (2021–23), we examine differences in …

title: Crossing borders, shaping careers: internationalization of labour in Japan?
abstract: Abstract Since the 1990s, Japan has pursued internationalization (kokusaika) as a key strategy to address economic stagnation, demographic decline, and growing labour shortages. This introduction situates the special issue within these broader transformations by conceptualising the internationalization of labour as a multi-layered and contested process. It highlights two central and interrelated policy trajectories: the internationalization of education aimed at fostering transnational human capital, and the selective expansion of labour migration. While both strategies have increased …

title: Feeling machines: Japanese robotics and the global entanglements of more-than-human care , by Shawn Bender
abstract: Having spent months observing daily routines in Japanese and French elder care homes and speaking with both care workers and roboticists for my 2025 research, I approached Shawn Bender’s Feeling Machines: Japanese Robotics and the Global Entanglements of More-Than-Human Care with a mixture of ethnographic familiarity and theoretical depth. Drawing on cultural anthropology, science and technology studies (STS), and human–robot interaction, Bender describes the lived experiences of actors in care automation. The author traces how Japanese kaigo robotto (care robots), engineered to sense affect …

title: The failure of political opposition in Japan: implications for democracy and a vision of the future , by Arthur Stockwin
abstract: There are few issues within the study of Japanese democracy that are more flummoxing than the continued failure of the opposition to mount a credible challenge against the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP). It is, after all, a perfectly packaged puzzle: here is a parliamentary democracy with no direct impediments imposed on its opposition or on its voters, and yet, the nation has almost continuously been governed by the same party since 1955. And this in spite of a long-term decline in the LDP’s popularity and power. Indeed, it has been clear since the LDP’s return to power in 2012 that its …

title: Rokujūnen anpo tōsō to chishikijin, gakusei, rōdōsha: Shakai undō no rekishi shakaigaku (the 1960 Anpo struggle and intellectuals, students, and workers: a historical sociology of social movements), by Saruya Hiroe.
abstract: The protests of 1959–60 against the revision of the US–Japan Security Treaty were the largest in Japan’s postwar history, yet there have been relatively few book-length attempts to explain, rather than simply narrate, how they came about. Saruya Hiroe’s book, a Japanese version of her 2012 dissertation at the University of Michigan, seeks to address this gap. The book draws on eighteen months of fieldwork and almost a hundred interviews with former student activists, trade unionists and academics. Saruya’s core argument is that the Anpo struggle was in fact several movements, each with its …

title: Sandō, kyoyō, bōkan sareta Jimintō seiji—Naze Abe seiken wa chōki seiken to natta no ka , by Asano Takaaki
abstract: A defining feature of Japanese politics in the 2010s is the seemingly paradoxical success of the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP). Under the leadership of Abe Shinzō, the party shifted markedly to the right, particularly on foreign and security policy, with Abe consistently advocating constitutional revision and a substantial military buildup. Yet the LDP won a series of elections, remained in office, and enabled Abe to become the longest-serving prime minister in Japanese history—even though voters as a whole exhibited little evidence of a corresponding ideological shift. In this timely and …

title: What can economists contribute during a crisis? A review of COVID-19 economic research for policymaking in Japan
abstract: Abstract This survey article reviews economic research on the COVID-19 pandemic in Japan, focusing on how economists provided policy-relevant evidence while the crisis was still unfolding. Japan experienced lower infection and death rates than many other countries, and its containment measures relied mainly on requests rather than legal restrictions. Even so, the pandemic caused large economic disruptions and exposed problems in medical capacity and policy coordination. The review highlights several findings. Voluntary behavioural responses to information and perceived risk played an …

Cold War cattle, dairy farming, and transnational development cooperation in South Korea during the 1960s/70s

With the technical and financial cooperation of the Australian, Canadian, Danish, Japanese, New Zealand, and West German governments, the Korean actors imported livestock, established model farms, and conducted research projects on grassland and forage. title: Temples and markets – Buddhism and life insurance in Meiji Japan
abstract: Life insurance established itself in Japan as a domestic industry by the end of the Meiji period. A unique feature of the early years of the industry was the emergence of Buddhist-related life insurance companies from 1894 onwards. However, by 1914, these companies had either gone out of business or restructured and ceased their affiliation with Buddhism. Japanese research explains the entry of Buddhist sects into life insurance with reference to their financial needs, while their disappearance 20 years later is attributed to lack of technical expertise and weak corporate governance. This …

title: Sur la voie d’une histoire des laideurs
abstract: Partant d’une réflexion artistique, celle du sculpteur Auguste Rodin sur la laideur, l’article questionne l’historiographie de la laideur, par un retour sur les études sur les corps antiques parues depuis une vingtaine d’années. En effet, l’histoire de la laideur ou plutôt des laideurs s’inscrit pour partie dans celle sur le corps (en particulier les corps ravagés, malmenés, maltraités, handicapés), qu’elle dépasse cependant. L’histoire des émotions ou celle des animaux sont aussi des pistes récentes qui peuvent être convoquées pour aborder la question de la laideur.

title: ‘M’ aghan cri, coir, gradhach’ – ‘My heifer beloved, kind and loving’: human-cattle relationships and the Highland Clearances in the nineteenth-century Scottish Gàidhealtachd
abstract: This thesis examines the impact of the Highland Clearances on human-cattle relationships in the Scottish Gàidhealtachd in the nineteenth century. Primarily through a mixture of nineteenth-century Gaelic song poetry, the evidence given to the Royal Commission of Inquiry into the Condition of the Crofters and Cottars in the Highlands of Scotland (Napier Commission, 1884) and archival documents, it traces how human-cattle relationships shifted as a result of the disruption to small-scale subsistence practices wrought by the Highland Clearances (c. 1760-c. 1860). title: The Anthropocene in Contemporary History? Towards an Agenda for Local Historical Research in the Age of Authoritarian Regimes and Their Aftermath
abstract: Abstract The debate surrounding the term “Anthropocene” poses profound challenges for the discipline of contemporary history by demanding new standards and scales. Drawing on concepts for a more-than-human-history and a multitemporal approach, the research model in this chapter is based on the concept of a “contaminated history” (Maß 2024), in which every research on contemporary history incorporates global interconnections and non-human actors. The chapter discusses the possibilities for contemporary Anthropocene research using the crisis of democracy in the small Thuringian town of Geisa …

abstract: Southern Scandinavian and Scanian settlement archaeology has in the past four decades been able to highlight overarching shifts in prehistoric and especially Iron Age settlement organisation, and thus developed methods of rigorous typo-chronological analyses. abstract: This article examines the contributions of Doctor of Historical Sciences and Professor Sergey Ilyich Kuznetsov to historical scholarship, education, and the development of international relations at Irkutsk State University. The authors highlight key stages in Kuznetsov's development as an orientalist, drawing the reader's attention to his most important publications. The article outlines the main areas of Kuznetsov's research and his results, recognized in the Russian and international academic community. It also describes Sergey Ilyich's contribution to the development of the Irkutsk State …

abstract: The article traces the processes related to the development of the staff that provides the teaching of modern and contemporary Bulgarian history at St. Cyril and St. Methodius University of Veliko Tarnovo from its establishment to the present day. The presentation addresses the issues related to the creation and functioning of the Department of Modern and Contemporary Bulgarian History, the implementation of educational and research activities, as well as the leadership of student scientific initiatives by the department members.

abstract: The town of Fushimi is rarely seen as a part of Kyoto. Yet, from the fall of Toyotomi Hideyoshi’s Momoyama Castle in 1600, to the Battle of Toba-Fushimi in 1868, the town’s history was key to the fate of Kyoto, and Japan. In the twentieth century, the Meiji emperor was buried on the grounds of Fushimi Castle, the Nogi Shrine was dedicated nearby, and the imperial army took over large swathes of the town, making Fushimi an important site for military and imperial pilgrimage and activities. Before 1945, a visit to Fushimi was an important site for school groups. Much of this history disappeared …

title: Plants in the Shade
abstract: The now-archaic botanical term "cryptogam" was used to refer to ferns, mushrooms, and other plants thought to reproduce without producing seeds. In Japanese, however, the term cryptogam (inka shokubutsu) has been used as a metaphor for queer sexualities since shortly after World War II. Starting in the early 1950s, inka shokubutsu began to be used to refer to queer communities emerging in Tokyo and other urban centers and was subsequently adopted by mainstream media during the 1960s and 1970s. By the 1990s, however, the term had fallen out of use, as a new generation of LGBTQ activists argued …

title: The Nuclear Beautiful
abstract: Following seminal critical work by Frances Ferguson (1984) and Peter B. Hales (1991), many writers have invoked the aesthetic category of the sublime when describing artists' and observers' responses to nuclear weapons; the technical term has thus been the nuclear sublime. This article argues for the viability of a related but different aesthetic category: the nuclear beautiful. Twentieth-century creators working in various media represented a seemingly improbable aesthetic response to nuclear explosions: under certain circumstances, a spectator might find beauty in a nuclear detonation and …

title: Kyoto's Universities at War, 1937-1945
abstract: The development of Japan's university sector was a key factor in Japan's modernization process after the Meiji Restoration. The period from the 1870s to 1940s was also a period of Japanese imperialism, and from the 1930s, militarism. As a result, many of Japan's oldest and most prestigious universities, both national/public and private, made important scientific, social, and intellectual contributions to imperialism and militarism. This article examines how three prestigious universities in Kyoto—Kyoto University, Ritsumeikan University, and Doshisha University—have presented their wartime …

title: The Transnational Samurai
abstract: This article explores the reception and appropriation of the Japanese samurai in Italian nationalist and Fascist discourse from the early twentieth century to the far-right movements of the 1960s and 1970s. Through a close examination of figures such as Luigi Barzini Sr., Shimoi Harukichi, Giuseppe Tucci, and Julius Evola, it analyzes how the ethical code of bushido, popularized in Europe through Inazō Nitobe’s Bushido: The Soul of Japan, was interpreted by Italian writers through the lens of Classical Roman ideals of honorable death, civic duty, and heroic virtue. The article emphasizes an …

title: “The Supreme Command of Our Forces is in Our Hands”
abstract: The Restoration Edict of January 1868, which restored the political power of the emperor, was followed by a series of measures that abolished the warrior class (bushi) and established the supremacy of the imperial court in military matters. Drawing on ancient history and mythology, such as the military campaigns of Japan’s first (legendary) Emperor Jinmu, imperial apologists vilified the warrior class and accused it of “usurping” imperial authority for more than five hundred years. In this article, I show that the Imperial Japanese Army took a rather condescending view of the warrior rule of …

title: Samurai in Southeast Asia
abstract: In the early 1600s, various commercial entrepots in maritime Southeast Asia became home to Japanese mercenaries, merchants, and exiled Christians. Their sociopolitical roles in Southeast Asia, and their subsequent exploitation by different (memory) regimes, emphasizes these Japanese as exceptional historical actors and contributes to the trope of the samurai within early modern historiography. Focusing on two icons of this early modern southward expansion—Takayama Ukon, commemorated as “Christ’s samurai,” and Yamada Nagamasa, labeled “the Samurai of Ayutthaya”—this article explores the …

abstract: Tourist media often presents Kyoto as ancient and tranquil, and thus as distanced from modern war and international politics. However, postwar Kyoto has had a clear diplomatic role, including as a home to international war memorials. This article examines one of these memorials—Ryōzen Kannon, a Buddhist site built in the 1950s to commemorate Japanese and foreign war dead. Its primary focus is a 1962 tour to Ryōzen Kannon by veterans of the 100th Battalion, a famed U.S. Army unit composed primarily of soldiers of Japanese descent from Hawai‘i. The article begins by exploring how Ryōzen …

abstract: This research note investigates competing strategies of reproduction employed in modern Japanese books with reference to three specific volumes. The first is the Overview of Useful Lumber (Yūyō mokuzai shōran) published in 1874; the second is an early chromolithographic publication, the Chōyōkaku Appreciations: Brocades Section (Chōyōkaku kanshō, kinshū no bu) of 1883; and the third is a deluxe facsimile of an early-modern album of treasured calligraphy known as the Verdure tekagami (Tekagami nobe no midori) from 1972.
